what: Lithia Motors sells cars. It is one of the largest car dealership groups in the United States, selling new and used vehicles, servicing them, and financing them through its own lender, Driveway Finance. It also runs the Driveway and GreenCars online platforms and a large Canadian and UK operation.
customers: Car buyers across North America and the United Kingdom, plus service customers returning for maintenance and repair, and manufacturers who need retail distribution.
money: Franchised new car sales across most major manufacturer brands.
Used retail and wholesale, sourced largely from trade-ins and lease returns.
Workshop labour and parts, plus finance and insurance commission and interest from its own lending arm.
moat: Dealership franchise rights are granted by manufacturers and protected by state franchise laws, which makes them licences rather than businesses that can be competed into existence. Service and parts generate high-margin recurring revenue from vehicles already sold, and the finance arm keeps the lending profit that the group would otherwise hand to a bank. Scale allows Lithia to buy dealerships from retiring owners at prices smaller groups cannot match.
risks: Reported debt of about $10.6B against $391.3M of cash is large, though much of it is floor-plan financing secured on vehicle inventory and the loan book of the finance arm.
Free cash flow was about negative $426.7M as the finance arm grew its loan book, which consumes cash before it produces interest income.
Owning a subprime-leaning captive lender adds credit risk that pure dealers do not carry, and loss rates rise with unemployment.
New vehicle gross margins have normalised sharply from the shortage years, which removes the windfall that made the last few years look so good.
Growth has been built on continuous acquisition, and paying too much for dealerships late in the cycle is the classic way these groups destroy value.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $22.8B in 2021 to $37.6B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $38.2B.
The shares trade at about 8.3 times earnings and 0.16 times sales.
Service and parts revenue grows with the number of vehicles the group has sold, is largely recession-resistant, and carries far higher margins than selling cars.
Fifteen analysts average a $391.20 target, about 35% above the current price.
The dealership market remains fragmented and family-owned, so there is a long supply of acquisitions available from owners without successors.
watch: Service and parts gross profit, and the credit performance of Driveway Finance. New car margins will keep normalising; the workshop and the loan book determine what the group is actually worth.
view: Car dealerships are a much better business than their reputation suggests, and Lithia has been the most aggressive consolidator in it. The reason the model works is that three different businesses sit inside one building: a low-margin, cyclical new-car business that brings people through the door, a high-margin workshop that earns money on every car ever sold, and a finance and insurance desk that takes a commission on the transaction. The franchise rights are protected by state law, so nobody competes them away. Buy enough of these, run them better than the retiring families who owned them, and you compound.

At 8.3 times earnings the market is clearly not paying for that compounding, and there are two defensible reasons why. The first is that the last few years were abnormally good: vehicle shortages let dealers sell above list price, and new-car gross margins reached levels nobody expected to hold. They are normalising, and earnings that were flattered by scarcity are now being compared against themselves. Anyone extrapolating the shortage-era margin is going to be disappointed, and a single-digit multiple is partly the market saying so.

The second reason is Driveway Finance, and this is where I would spend my time. Lithia chose to keep the lending profit rather than hand it to a bank, which is sensible when credit is good and expensive when it is not. It is why free cash flow was negative $427 million in the trailing year — a growing loan book consumes cash before it pays interest — and it is why the $10.6 billion debt figure looks alarming until you separate floor-plan financing and the loan book from genuine corporate borrowing. Done well this adds a durable earnings stream. Done badly, in a downturn, a captive lender to car buyers is exactly where losses appear first and largest. The credit metrics on that book matter more to the next three years than anything about car volumes.

My overall read: a genuinely good collection of protected local businesses, bought at a cyclically fair price rather than a bargain, with a finance arm that is either an underappreciated asset or the thing that hurts. The fifteen analysts at $391.20 are underwriting normalised margins plus continued acquisition. I would be more interested in the boring part of the income statement: service and parts gross profit, which grows mechanically with every car the group has ever sold and does not care what the economy does. If that line keeps compounding while the loan book behaves, the current multiple is too low. If credit turns, nothing else will matter.
bull: Service and parts gross profit compounds with the installed base, acquisitions keep adding protected franchises cheaply, and the finance arm proves a durable extra earnings stream.
bear: New-car margins keep normalising into a consumer slowdown while credit losses in Driveway Finance arrive at the same time, against $10.6 billion of borrowings.
